outlooks.summary: Severe thunderstorms capable of damaging winds and a tornado threat are expected across much of the Florida Peninsula today, and in eastern portions of the Carolinas later this afternoon into tonight.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Models remain consistent with the evolution of the mid-upper level flow pattern this forecast period, as very strong 12-hour 500-mb height falls are expected to occur from the Southeast states into the upper Ohio Valley region. A full-latitude trough, now extending into the western Gulf Basin, will shift east today, while a 100-110-kt 500-mb jet rounds its base, with the greatest height falls expected this evening through the overnight. In response, strengthening southerly low-level winds, with a broad zone of 50-kt 850-mb flow extending from FL to the Carolinas and into VA by afternoon, will transport moisture poleward with mid 60s surface dew points across much of the FL Peninsula. A synoptic low should track across GA into the central Appalachians. Given this track of the low and strengthening low-level winds, the coastal/marine boundary is expected to move inland across parts eastern SC/NC, allowing for an increase in moisture.

sections.title: FL Peninsula
sections.text: Current trends in lightning data indicated at least two bands of thunderstorms, associated along a cold front, which will advance east across the FL Peninsula today. Extensive cloud cover preceding the cold front and the lack of steep lapse rates are two factors that will limit the likelihood for stronger destabilization today. However, models do suggest the strongest buoyancy should be located across the west-central FL Peninsula by early afternoon. Given the juxtaposition of MLCAPE around 1000 J/kg and strong low- and deep-layer shear, the higher severe probabilities have been expanded westward. CAMs suggest several bands of storms (QLCS mode) should advance across the FL Peninsula today. The initial band is expected to advance across north-central FL during the late morning, while the second band moves across the central peninsula this afternoon and early evening, posing the greatest severe-weather threat when instability will be the strongest. Although backed surface winds/hodograph curvature should be larger across west-central FL, a tornado threat also exists across the rest of the Slight risk area. sections.title: Northeast SC/eastern NC
sections.text: CAMs suggest the northern extent of the FL QLCS should move across eastern SC during the mid-late afternoon and through eastern NC this evening. Although instability will be marginal, strengthening low-level winds and subsequent increase of hodograph curvature will support a tornado threat and potential for damaging winds with the strongest organized storms.

sections.title: Southeast VA
sections.text: A marginal severe risk is maintained into southeast VA where mainly elevated thunderstorms will be possible later this evening into Thursday night. Forecast soundings suggested a low probability for near-surface-based storms that could pose a threat for a brief tornado and/or damaging wind threat. ..Peters/Nauslar.. 12/20/2018

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: In mid/upper levels, a series of vorticity maxima will dig into an already high-amplitude/full-latitude synoptic trough, currently located from northwest ON across MN, IA, eastern OK, east TX, and the western Gulf down across the Bay of Campeche. By the end of the period, the trough should be located from the upper Great Lakes across AL to the Yucatan Peninsula vicinity, with anomalously low heights and intense height gradients at low latitudes. The net result will be a slight broadening and intensification of the cyclonic flow field across the Gulf. The 250-mb jet should increase from the 110-120 kt range over the eastern Gulf and FL at 00Z to 130-150 kt from northern FL to the eastern Carolinas by 12Z. At the surface, 11Z analysis showed the main frontal-wave low over the MOB area with a secondary/weaker low near TLH, amidst a broader, diffuse area of low pressure covering much of MS/AL southward over the Gulf. A cold front was drawn from the MOB-area low southward across the central gulf then southwestward to the southwestern Gulf. Two warm fronts were evident: 1. sections.title: FL
sections.text: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms are expected to move northeastward across the outlook area through this evening in two primary bands: 1. Morning activity now over the TBW/SRQ areas and extending southwestward across the Gulf. A marginal tornado threat exists in the next hour or two with this activity as it moves inland. 2. A longer band in both spatial length and timespan, expected to consolidate over the Gulf and west-central FL behind the morning convection and initially ahead of the front. This evening and overnight, the front should catch up and cause some eastward acceleration of the resulting QLCS as a whole across the remainder of eastern/southern FL. Following the morning activity, the main band should move into an increasingly high-thetae air mass over southwest, east-central and southeast FL. Meanwhile, over central FL, this QLCS will have more limited recovery time with weaker buoyancy. A moist, southerly Caribbean return-flow fetch will serve both to destabilize the boundary layer and keep winds backed enough to maintain favorably large low-level hodographs. sections.title: Eastern Carolinas to southeastern VA this evening
sections.text: A prefrontal band of strong-severe thunderstorms -- at least loosely manifesting the northern extension of the FL activity -- is expected to sweep north-northeastward across the Atlantic off GA and parts of SC, crossing coastal northeastern SC and eastern NC this evening into tonight. Damaging winds are the main concern, and a tornado threat also exists. Though the most-unstable boundary layer will remain over the Atlantic, partially modified marine air will spread somewhat inland across this region, amidst modest but sufficient lapse rates to support roughly 200-600 J/kg MLCAPE. Though instability will be marginal, and diminishing with northward extent across eastern NC into VA, sufficiently intense deep-layer winds, and both flow and shear in the lowest few km above the surface, will support a 15%/slight-risk-level wind-damage threat wherever unstable surface-based parcels are present, and a marginal threat farther north into very shallow layers of weak near-surface static stability. ..Edwards/Goss.. 12/20/2018

outlooks.summary: Damaging thunderstorm winds and tornadoes are possible across much of the Florida Peninsula today, and in eastern portions of the Carolinas late afternoon into tonight.

sections.title: FL
sections.text: A band of strong/severe storms is affecting parts of the central FL Peninsula this morning, with several transient mesocyclones noted in the past few hours. Given the strong low level shear in place in this region, a few tornadoes and locally damaging wind gusts will remain possible through mid-afternoon. Please refer to Mesoscale Discussion #1717 for further details. Meanwhile, the primary squall line remains offshore but will begin to move inland soon. The air mass ahead of the line is generally undisturbed and is heating/destabilizing. Forecast soundings across the southern Peninsula suggest MLCAPE values of 1000-1500 J/kg will be common. Shear profiles are also quite impressive with 40-50 kt winds as low as 1000-1500m. This will support a risk of embedded bows and supercells along the line, capable of damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes. Therefore have adjusted the ENH area slightly southward and may include the remainder of south FL in later updates.

sections.title: SC/NC/VA
sections.text: No changes have been made to this portion of the outlook. Rapid strengthening of the surface low will result in impressive wind fields over the eastern Carolinas later today, but most storms are forecast to remain offshore. Nevertheless, the conditional threat of an organized storm affecting the coastal counties is sufficient to maintain the SLGT risk. ..Hart/Bunting.. 12/20/2018

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Given the expectation that severe/tornado risk will gradually increase through this morning and into the afternoon, tornado watch issuance will likely be required prior to 20/14Z.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: As a leading band of south-southwest- to north-northeast-oriented convection continues spreading inland between Tampa Bay and Charlotte Harbor on the west coast of Florida, offshore updrafts exhibiting low-level rotation continue to move onshore. This trend is expected to continue, with additional bands of convection to move across the eastern Gulf and inland as the day progresses -- bands currently evident over the eastern Gulf in satellite and lightning loops. While early-morning visible imagery shows extensive cloud cover across much of central and south Florida, modest destabilization of the boundary layer, along with continued moistening, should combine with a very favorably sheared lower and middle troposphere to support gradually increasing severe risk with time. Along with increasing risk for damaging winds, a few tornadoes will also become increasingly likely. Given this, expect tornado watch issuance to occur within the next hour or so.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Severe storms including supercells should remain focused along an outflow boundary, with tornadoes and damaging wind gusts possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Strong southerly flow in a warm advection regime is currently aiding lift as well as enhancing shear profiles across FL where storms are currently situated southwest-northeast across central FL. While northern portions of this line continue to shift east, southwestern parts are becoming stationary and/or lifting north. Meanwhile, upstream heating and moisture advection persists with MLCAPE in excess of 1200 J/kg. Through afternoon, strong low-level wind fields will persist while instability gradually increases. A corridor of tornado or damaging wind threat will likely consolidate near the aforementioned boundary, with a few supercells possible. Further, a cold front is consolidated just off the west coast, and will further aid lift and enhance storm coverage later today. Where this front intersects the other may be a favored location for tornado potential.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The severe threat persists for the watch area, with primarily a damaging wind threat. An isolated tornado remains possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Storms have become linear as the front and outflows have merged, and movement of the line currently has a substantial eastward component. Winds aloft are mainly parallel to the line, and objective analysis shows a general decrease in low-level helicity, in part due to substantial boundary layer mixing. As such, bowing segments will be capable of damaging winds, and brief areas of rotation may occur as well. A greater tornado threat would occur if the line could slow. Ahead of the line, scattered convective showers were deepening with heating, but these will have a lesser threat of severe weather compared to the main line as most of them remain decoupled from the surface layer. A supercell cannot be ruled out with this activity should a cell turn right of the mean motion. ..Jewell.. 12/20/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Thunderstorms offshore will begin to approach the coastal Carolinas by this evening with the potential for strong wind gusts and a tornado or two. Trends are being monitored for the possibility of a watch by 00Z/7 pm EST.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest mesoanalysis shows a warm front extending from southeast VA southwest across central SC. Regional radar composite shows widespread rain across the discussion area, with a north-south line of thunderstorms offshore of the NC/SC coast. Latest high-res guidance indicates these thunderstorms will approach the coast through this evening, with storms continuing to move north/northeast across eastern NC through the late evening hours. Largely unidirectional winds throughout the lower-mid troposphere will increase significantly in speeds through this evening, resulting in southerly deep-layer shear values of 50-65 kts. Concurrently, weak buoyancy will develop inland as slightly higher theta-e air advects northward. Thunderstorms moving inland and over adjacent coastal waters will be oriented in line segments posing a risk for damaging winds. Very strong low-level SRH in excess of 300 m2/s2 will support storm-scale rotation and the possibility for a tornado or two. Radar and environmental trends will continue to be monitored for the possibility of a watch by early evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: An overall weakening trend has been observed in the ongoing convection in WW 440. A small area of modest instability still exists over southeast Florida. A strong wind gust or two will be the main threats for the next hour or two.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Per regional radar mosaic imagery, the gust front along the line of storms from near West Palm Beach to the portions of the Florida Keys has moved out ahead of convection. As this has occurred, an overall weakening trend has been observed in the ongoing convection. This is particularly true in northern portions of WW 440 where instability is lower than points to the south. With 40-50 kts of flow within the 850-700 mb layer, potential for a strong wind gust will exist over far southeastern Florida where MLCAPE will be maximized at 1000-1500 J/kg. However, weak mid-level lapse rates, boundary-parallel deep layer shear, and a stabilizing boundary layer should limit overall storm intensity/organization. ..Wendt.. 12/20/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Near surface stability should hinder the potential for tornadoes even with relatively strong low-level wind fields in place. A strong/severe wind gust will still be possible with the strongest convective activity. A WW is not anticipated.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Over the past hour, trends in VWP hodographs from KLTX have shown a decrease in low-level SRH. As the core of the 850 mb low-level jet continues to move to the north/northeast, this trend should continue. Though objective mesoanalysis shows effective SRH values still in the 200-400 m2/s2 range, the 00Z MHX sounding shows a stable layer near the surface that should limit the overall potential for tornadoes. Furthermore, surface analysis has shown dewpoints dropping over the last 2 hours near the coast. The main threat with any ongoing convection will be limited to strong wind gusts, given the remaining 35-50 kt flow in the lowest 2 km of the troposphere. Trends will continue to be monitored, but a WW is not anticipated.
